prompt: Why does the gap between granted and used permissions grow on its own?
hint: Think about which change ever produces a ticket.

choices.text: AWS adds new actions to existing policies every year
choices.why: A wildcard does pick up new actions, but that is not the habit the lesson describes. People add grants and never remove them.

choices.text: A permission that causes no error never gets a ticket to remove it
choices.why: Right. Every grant solved a real problem; nothing ever complains about one that is too wide.

choices.text: Unused permissions are added automatically after ninety days
choices.why: Nothing is added automatically; every grant was somebody's decision.

choices.text: Policies stop being enforced once they are old
choices.why: Age changes nothing about enforcement; an old policy is enforced exactly as a new one.

prompt: Match each AWS record to the question it answers.
hint: Three kinds of record, three questions.

pairs.left: when an access key was last used

pairs.right: what would a policy built from real calls look like?

prompt: A review has time for one identity today. Which should it look at first?
hint: One kind of extra permission has no ceiling.

choices.text: The user with the longest policy document
choices.why: Length says little; a two-line policy can be the dangerous one, as dani's was.

choices.text: A user who can read three more buckets than its job needs
choices.why: That is a real gap, and a bounded one. The other kind is not bounded.

choices.text: Any identity that can write to IAM
choices.why: Right. Whoever can change permissions can grant themselves the rest.

choices.text: The identity created most recently, since it has had the least review
choices.why: Recency is no measure of risk; dani's user was months old.

prompt: Of the three records the lesson describes, which one does moto keep?
hint: The transcripts used it.

choices.text: The service last accessed report
choices.why: moto answered that call with an internal server error.

choices.text: When each access key was last used
choices.why: Right: get-access-key-last-used named the date, the service and the region.

choices.text: Access Analyzer's unused-access findings, computed from CloudTrail
choices.why: They do not exist in moto, and moto records no CloudTrail events either.

prompt: dani was disabled at the clinic's identity provider in March, and her key still worked in October. Why did disabling her not reach it?
hint: What connects an IAM user to the identity provider?

choices.text: Nothing connects an IAM user to the identity provider
choices.why: Right. The IAM user lives in the account and was outside the process that removes people.

choices.text: The identity provider takes a full year to reach every account
choices.why: Federation takes effect at the next sign-in; there is no delay of that kind.

choices.text: Her role session had been issued with the twelve-hour maximum
choices.why: Twelve hours would have ended in March. She had a key, not a session.

choices.text: Access keys cannot be disabled once a password exists
choices.why: Any key can be deactivated or deleted; nobody did.

prompt: A person is removed from the identity provider at 10:00. At 10:20 a request signed with their role session still succeeds. What explains it, and what limits the damage?
hint: Disabling stops one thing and not another.

choices.text: The removal failed silently, and it has to be repeated in the AWS console of every account
choices.why: The removal worked: no new sign-in is possible. The session predates it.

choices.text: A session already issued lasts until it expires; short sessions, or revoking older sessions, limit it
choices.why: Right. AWS documents a deny on sessions issued before a given time for exactly this.

choices.text: Role sessions never expire, so the role itself has to be deleted before the person loses access
choices.why: They expire, after fifteen minutes to twelve hours.

choices.text: MFA was not enforced at the provider
choices.why: MFA guards the sign-in, and the session already existed before the removal.

prompt: Match each IAM Identity Center piece to what it is.
hint: The table in the section, in sign-in order.

pairs.right: a named collection of policies, defined once
a group given a permission set in one account
what the person's session is a session of

right_distractors: a long-lived key for each person

prompt: Which identity should a review expect to find outside the identity provider, on purpose?
hint: For the day the provider is down.

choices.text: A user per developer, kept as a backup in case federation ever breaks
choices.why: That is the arrangement federation replaces, and twenty backups are twenty ways in.

choices.text: The CI pipeline's user, since a pipeline has no way to use federation at all
choices.why: Pipelines can assume roles through federation; lesson 4 shows it.

choices.text: One break-glass identity, with hardware MFA, alarmed on every use
choices.why: Right, and only one.

choices.text: Nobody: every identity has to go through the provider
choices.why: Then an outage at the provider would lock everybody out, including the people fixing it.

prompt: In the lab, what did `INITIAL_NO_AUTH_ACTION_COUNT=3` change?
hint: Before it, moto accepted any key.

choices.text: It limited every user to three requests
choices.why: There is no limit per user; three is how many requests pass before judging starts.

choices.text: It let three requests through unchecked, then judged every request
choices.why: Right. The three are spent creating the administrator.

choices.text: It created three users automatically, one of them an administrator
choices.why: You created admin yourself, with the three free requests.

choices.text: It made moto enforce conditions, boundaries and service control policies as well
choices.why: None of those are enforced even with checking on; identity policies are.

prompt: dani's policy allows only `iam:AttachUserPolicy` and `iam:ListAttachedUserPolicies` on `*`. Why was that enough to become an administrator?
hint: Which policy, attached to which user?

choices.text: Any policy could be attached to any user, hers included
choices.why: Right. Narrow-looking, and the right action with no limit on the policy or the user.

choices.text: ListAttachedUserPolicies reveals the administrator's key
choices.why: It lists policy names; it reveals no key.

choices.text: moto grants administrator rights to any user whose policy names IAM
choices.why: moto judged the policy as written; AWS would have done the same with it.

choices.text: A bug in AWS allowed it
choices.why: Nothing is wrong with AWS here; the permission did exactly what it says.

prompt: The attach request printed nothing. What does the lesson make of that?
hint: A silent prompt.

choices.text: Nothing, since a command with no output did nothing
choices.why: The next list-users succeeded where it had failed; something changed.

choices.text: That the request succeeded, and that silence is the finding
choices.why: Right. AWS gives no warning for a permission used as granted.

choices.text: That moto failed to log the request, so it cannot be proved
choices.why: The proof is the next request: list-users, refused before, answered after.

choices.text: That the request is still pending an approval from admin
choices.why: IAM has no approval step; a request is allowed or refused.

prompt: Which changes, each on its own, would have closed dani's path? Choose all that apply.
hint: Remove any one link.

choices.text: Deleting her IAM user when she left
choices.why: Right: no user, no path.

choices.text: Deleting her access key
choices.why: Right: the request needed a working key.

choices.text: Limiting the policy to the one policy she was meant to attach
choices.why: Right, with a condition on `iam:PolicyARN`, which AWS enforces and moto does not.

choices.text: Giving bia ReadOnlyAccess instead of a wider policy
choices.why: bia was never on the path.

choices.text: Turning on MFA for admin
choices.why: Good practice, and irrelevant to a request signed with dani's key.

prompt: Where did the script take its list of risky IAM actions from?
hint: Guessing is how a list misses one.

choices.text: From a list of the ten most common mistakes on a security blog
choices.why: The lesson took it from AWS itself.

choices.text: From the quarantine policy AWS attaches to an exposed key
choices.why: Right: AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantineV3, whose first statement denied 98 actions.

choices.text: From the error messages moto printed during the lesson
choices.why: Error messages name one action at a time, and only the ones refused.

choices.text: From the credential report
choices.why: The report covers passwords, MFA and keys, not permissions.

prompt: How many actions did the first statement of `AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantineV3` deny in moto's copy?
hint: grep -c counted them.

prompt: A user holds a policy allowing `iam:Put*` on `*`. The lesson's script prints nothing for it. Why, and is the user safe?
hint: Read the script's limits.

choices.text: It is safe: Put actions only add data, they never grant anything
choices.why: `iam:PutUserPolicy` writes an inline policy, which can grant anything.

choices.text: The script reads only managed policies, and this grant sits in an inline policy instead
choices.why: It reads inline policies too; dani's inline one was printed.

choices.text: Exact-string matching misses the wildcard; the user still writes policies
choices.why: Right. A clean run of a script with known blind spots is not a clean account.

choices.text: moto does not support wildcards in actions
choices.why: The question is about the script's match, not moto; the script is plain jq.

prompt: caio's `PowerUserAccess` is written with `NotAction` excluding `iam:*`. Why did the script stay silent about it, and why is that silence not a guarantee in general?
hint: What does a NotAction allow?

choices.text: Right by luck: it never reads that field, so a different list would pass unseen
choices.why: Right. The script never reads NotAction at all; it happened to be right about this one.

choices.text: Because PowerUserAccess is maintained by AWS, and the script skips every policy that AWS maintains itself
choices.why: It reads attached managed policies; AdministratorAccess was printed.

choices.text: Because caio has no access key
choices.why: The script reads policies, not keys.

choices.text: Because NotAction policies are refused by AWS
choices.why: AWS accepts them; its own PowerUserAccess is one.

prompt: In the lab, dani's key was set to `Inactive` and the next request it signed still succeeded. What should you conclude?
hint: Here the lab is wrong.

choices.text: Deactivating a key is useless, on AWS exactly as in moto, so the step can be skipped
choices.why: AWS refuses requests signed with an inactive key; moto does not.

choices.text: moto does not honour inactive keys; AWS does, by its documentation
choices.why: Right, and deleting the key is the step that holds in both.

choices.text: The change takes several minutes to reach every endpoint, so the key still worked
choices.why: list-access-keys already showed it Inactive; moto simply ignores the status.

choices.text: The status was not saved, so the command must be repeated
choices.why: It was saved: list-access-keys printed Inactive.

prompt: Put the steps of closing dani's path in the order the lesson uses.
hint: Close the way in before tidying.
trap: Starting with the policies is the slip: a key that still works can put them back.

prompt: `aws iam delete-user --user-name dani` answered `DeleteConflict`. What did it want first?
hint: Read the error.

choices.text: Her policies deleted
choices.why: Right: the inline manage-users was still on the user.

choices.text: Approval from a second administrator
choices.why: IAM has no approval step.

choices.text: Her MFA device to be registered so that the deletion could be confirmed
choices.why: No MFA is involved in deleting a user.

choices.text: A wait of seven days after deactivating her key
choices.why: There is no waiting period for a user; the error named the policies.

prompt: Match each guardrail to what it does.
hint: None of the three is enforced by moto.

pairs.right: limits which policies may be attached
a ceiling on one user or role
a deny across the whole organisation

prompt: Which of these did moto 5.2.3 get right in this lesson, as AWS would? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of them it got wrong or did not do.

choices.text: Refusing dani's list-users before she had the administrator policy
choices.why: Right: an implicit deny, judged from her identity policy.

choices.text: Allowing her attach-user-policy, as her policy said
choices.why: Right: AWS would have allowed it too.

choices.text: Refusing a request signed with an inactive key
choices.why: moto accepted it; AWS refuses.

choices.text: Refusing a request signed with a deleted key
choices.why: Right: InvalidClientTokenId.

choices.text: Producing an Access Advisor report
choices.why: It answered with an internal server error.

prompt: A role session lasts at most ___ hours.
hint: The role's maximum session duration has a ceiling.

prompt: A new contractor must hand one specific managed policy to new analysts, and nothing else. Which grant fits on AWS?
hint: dani's policy, with the missing limit added.

choices.text: `iam:*` limited to the analysts' group, so the grant reaches nobody outside it
choices.why: `iam:*` includes writing policies; scoping it to a group does not stop the escalation.

choices.text: `iam:AttachUserPolicy` on `*`, exactly as dani had it, plus a reminder to review it
choices.why: That is the path this lesson closed.

choices.text: `iam:AttachUserPolicy` with a condition on `iam:PolicyARN` naming that ARN
choices.why: Right. AWS enforces it; moto would not, so this one is proved from the documentation.

choices.text: AdministratorAccess, with a note in the ticket to remove it later
choices.why: Later is the gap this lesson measured.
